No fine. The Danish DPA reported JobTeam A/S to the police and recommended DKK 50,000; the district court acquitted the company. In Denmark the data protection authority cannot fine: it reports the case to the police and recommends an amount, and a court sets the fine.

The Belgian Data Protection Authority's Litigation Chamber examined the 'invite a friend' feature of the social network W, which uploaded users' phone and email contacts, including non-members, and sent invitation emails. It found that the controller had no valid legal basis for processing non-members' data (it had relied on the users' consent and, later, on a legitimate interest argument it had not raised earlier), and that invitation emails were sent to existing members while recipients were pre-ticked by default, so consent was not valid. It imposed a fine of EUR 50,000, taking account of the deliberate nature and the gravity of the breach, the removal of pre-ticked boxes and the end of the invitation emails.

INPS notified the Garante of two personal data breaches that occurred around 31 March to 2 April 2020, when many users tried to access its portal for COVID-19 benefits. The first was a misconfigured CDN cache that let some users see other people's registry data; the second was a flaw in the Bonus Baby Sitting application procedure that let unauthorised users view, change, delete or submit other users' applications concerning minors. The Garante ordered INPS under Article 58(2)(e) to notify all affected data subjects without delay and within 15 days, and asked for documented proof within 20 days. No fine was imposed; the Garante reserved the right to take further, including sanctioning, measures once the investigation is complete.

A complainant alleged that a lawyer at Síminn hf. sent an email about him to other staff and that Síminn refused his request for a copy of that email. Síminn denied that any such email was sent. The Authority found it was word against word and could not establish that the processing took place, so it could not say the complainant's rights under Act No. 90/2018 had been breached. It also noted that Síminn answered the access request within the one-month time limit. The decision found no violation.

A prison officer asked the Prison and Probation Service for access to all reports naming him, including reports on use of force and cell placements. The service first refused, saying only reports he had written could be searched. After the Danish DPA intervened, it found and disclosed the reports, but only later than it should have. The DPA issued criticism under the access provision of the Law Enforcement Act (§ 15). It also accepted that the request to search free-text fields across about 8-10 million documents could be refused under § 19 of that Act.

A complaint led the Swedish authority to examine the Örebro County health board. Between September 2019 and January 2020, the board published on the region's open website a full complaint to the Parliamentary Ombudsman (JO) that contained a patient's personal identity number, contact details, and health data (forced psychiatric admission and a urine drug test). The authority found that the publication had no purpose, legal basis or exception under the sensitive-data ban, that the national identification number was published unlawfully, and that the board lacked written publishing routines. It imposed an administrative fine of SEK 120,000 and ordered the board to adopt written instructions and routines for publishing personal data on open websites.

A data leak occurred when an Indian processor, working under a 2014 IT services contract with the Belgian defendant, copied a production database with order history to a cloud server. The server was left open to the internet, exposing personal data of 32,153 customers from 22 March to 28 May 2018. The defendant notified the leak to the authority in June 2018, and the inspection service then examined risk assessment (Articles 5, 24, 32, 33, 34) and the timing of the processor contract (Article 28). On Article 28 the Chamber found that the contract, drafted before the GDPR applied but signed only afterwards, did not breach the rules, and the operative part orders a dismissal (non-lieu) of the case. No fine was imposed.

The Cypriot Data Protection Authority held that the footage from a CCTV system of an individual shall be handled as subject to Article 4(1) of the GDPR Regulation. The meaning of that conclusion is that the Data Controller is obligated to provide access to the affected individual.

The Estonian DPA (AKI) ordered an apartment association to cease the disclosure of photos depicting members of the association in places where third parties had access, without obtaining prior consent. It also imposed € 500 fine as injunction.

A complainant doubted the legitimacy of a 2018 consultation of her photo in the Belgian National Register by an employee of a city. The city could not justify the access, because its access log did not record the purpose of the consultation, despite the authority's Recommendation 07/2017 requiring that. The Chambre Contentieuse found breaches of the accountability, security and purpose principles and imposed a reprimand, noting that the city said the failings had since been remedied and that it cooperated well. The access itself predated the GDPR, but the later failures fell within the authority's competence.
The Litigation Chamber of the Belgian DPA imposed a €50,000 fine on a company for non-compliance with the requirements relating to the appointment and function of a DPO under the GDPR.

The Swedish DPA fined Statens servicecenter (SSC), which acted as processor for 47 public authorities and as controller for its own staff, for late breach notification. A flaw in the Primula HR system let users see personal data of about 282,000 people; SSC found out on 28 March 2019 but notified the authorities only in August 2019 and the DPA only in June 2019. The DPA imposed fines of SEK 150,000 (Art. 33(2)) and SEK 50,000 (Art. 33(1)), found a breach of Art. 33(5) without a fine, and ordered SSC to set up breach documentation routines.

The Romanian supervisory authority completed an investigation into Telekom Romania Communications SA on 23 April 2020. A complainant said contracts had been fraudulently concluded in his name. The authority found the company lacked sufficient security measures, in particular checks on the accuracy of personal data collected by phone, so new subscription contracts were made using data from an existing contract without verification, breaching Article 32 GDPR. The company was fined 14,524.2 lei (stated as EUR 3,000) and ordered to put in place effective identification procedures, regular staff training and periodic compliance checks.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) opined that an insurance company is entitled to ask personal data when it is necessary to justify an insurance claim but it could not assess if this would be necessary and proportionate for information dated five years ago.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued the non-binding opinion that the personal data of researchers employed by a public institute is in principle not personal data but publicly available information. However, a concrete assessment about the nature of this and the legal basis has to be made by the data controller.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued a non-binding opinion about apps which would track the state of health and the movements of confirmed patients with SARS-CoV-2. The IP opined that a DPIA would be mandatory and that EU member states should coordinate their actions regarding such apps.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued a non-binding opinion about employees' personal data that an employer can process during work from home. The IP emphasised that the principles of data minimisation and transparency must be respected as well as the information obligations according to Articles 13 and 14 GDPR.

A complainant said a shop's exterior 'globe 360°' cameras filmed him on the pavement in September 2018 without consent or signage. The Inspectorate found the cameras had not been properly declared to the privacy commission before going live, and that the shop had no complete record of processing activities. The Litigation Chamber found breaches of the camera law declaration duty and of Article 30(1) GDPR together with the camera-law record requirement, and issued a reprimand with an order to establish a full record of processing within 3 months.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued a non-binding opinion regarding the processing of personal data of teachers and pupils when new technologies are used in order to offer or participate in a lesson. The IP opined that data controllers (i.e. schools) should seek for an adequate legal basis and pay attention in particular to their information obligation, the security of personal data, possible data transfers to the US and the principle of data minimisation.

ANSPDCP announced that it concluded an investigation into Banca Comercială Română S.A. on 14 April 2020 following a complaint. It found the bank had not implemented adequate technical and organisational security measures. Copies of identity documents of customers, including minors and their legal representatives, were collected via an employee's personal phone and sent internally via WhatsApp, contrary to the bank's internal procedure. The bank was fined RON 24,163.50, equivalent to EUR 5,000.

The Bulgarian DPA fined a political party about €1000 (BGN 2000) for processing personal data without a legal ground as required by Article 6(1) GDPR, after hiring a handwriting expert to determine that an alleged signature was fake.

On April 14, 2020, the ICO supported the decision of the Insolvency Service to withold the information it held about insolvent companies. Furthermore, it stated that the confirmation or denial by the Insolvency Serivce that it held more information about the companies within the scope of the request invovled the disclosure of personal data itself.

The Romanian DPA closed an investigation into Estee Lauder Romania SRL on 10 April 2020 and found it had breached Articles 6, 7 and 9 GDPR. The case began with a complaint about unlawful processing: disclosure and collection of personal data, including health information, without consent or another legal basis. The controller was fined RON 14,483.4, stated to be the equivalent of EUR 3,000. It was also ordered, as a corrective measure under Art. 58(2)(d), to bring its collection and further processing into compliance by regularly training its staff.

The Slovenian Data Protection Authority (IP) issued an advisory opinion on the lawfulness of a telephone application which would track individuals for the containment of the COVID-19 spread. The IP stressed that any such solution should respect the Constitution, the GDPR, the the Electronic Communications Act (ZEKom-1) and the Data Protection Act (ZVOP-1) and its effectiveness should be assessed in advance.
